item.title: GT Voice: Hyping supremacy of US chips is too narcissistic
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-22 23:12:00
Production of semiconductor chip File photo: VCG The Wall Street Journal recently portrayed Chinese AI companies as suffering "withdrawal" pains because of what it described as an "addiction" to Nvidia chips, claiming that US moves to cut off China's access to advanced computing power would deal "a blow to Beijing's artificial-intelligence ambitions." It seems that quite a few US media outlets are playing a game of distortion, giving far too much credit to American chip technology, and far too little to China's AI capabilities. This is less a reflection of China's AI industry than a political narrative designed to sway US public opinion. By overstating the impact of chip restrictions, the narrative appears designed to give the anti-China hawks fresh ammunition for pushing tighter export controls. But the narrative is itself fundamentally flawed: it serves America's domestic political battles, rather than reflecting the realities of China's AI development. Some anti-China hawks are eager to convince the public that tighter US chip controls can cripple China's AI industry progress, and they need arguments to build support for further restrictions. Yet they have little hard evidence to substantiate such claims. Instead, they need rhetoric such as "Chinese addiction" to give their case greater traction. But China's semiconductor industry is no work of fiction to be written at will. It is following its own course, making steady progress through sustained efforts. The fact is that many US media commentaries are increasingly out of touch with the realities of China's technology industry. In a media interview in December 2025, Liu Qingfeng, chairperson of iFlytek, said that without using domestic computing power to train large-language models, there would always be a major weakness that could not be overcome, along with a lack of security guarantees for long-term development. Liu said that his company had taken considerable resolve and made great efforts to train its own large-language models on domestic computing power, so as to avoid being held hostage by others. This points to a change in China's approach to technological self-reliance. Developing indigenous capabilities is no longer merely a reluctant response to US chip restrictions, but an active choice by Chinese companies as they look to the next stage of growth. The objective is not simply to find alternatives when access to foreign technology is restricted, but to build a more secure foundation for the industry's future. Ironically, successive rounds of US chip restrictions have helped accelerate this process. China's AI industry is increasingly capable of pursuing greater security across its supply chain, and this is a choice it has both the means and the incentive to make. Against this backdrop, the marginal impact of further US export controls on China's AI industry is diminishing rapidly. Whatever form the restrictions take, they are always ineffective at dictating the course of China's AI development. A striking contrast in tone has emerged. In parts of the US media environment, the language is one of "withdrawal" and "addiction." Chinese industry leaders, by contrast, speak of the need for security, the sustained effort required to build indigenous capabilities, and the practical demands of long-term development. This contrast exposes how detached the anti-China hawks have become from the realities of China's technology industry. Jensen Huang's resignation as Nvidia CEO appears to have further emboldened some anti-China hawks, who trumpeted for a tougher line against China, with some US media outlets adding to the chorus. Some commentaries have paid scant attention to the damage tighter export controls would inflict on the US chip industry itself. The restrictions will ultimately weaken those companies' position in the global markets. The US industry may ultimately have to swallow the bitter consequences. Whatever the US rhetoric, China's AI industry is moving forward. Some challenges are inevitable, but they are hardly the "withdrawal" pains portrayed by some US media organizations. The course of China's efforts to build its own chip and AI capabilities is clear. The more aggressively anti-China hawks push for restrictions, the faster China may move to strengthen those capabilities. The addiction that needs to be broken is not in China's AI industry. It is the political habit of the anti-China hawks of turning hostility toward China into political capital, and the blind faith among some US media commentators in America's technological supremacy. They ought to take a clear-eyed look at China's industrial progress, the complementary strengths of the two countries' AI industries, and the potential for both to benefit from cooperation.

item.title: The world is talking about Shenzhen – what are they talking about?: Global Times editorial
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-22 21:52:00
APEC China 2026. Illustration: Liu Rui/GT Viewed from the world's perspective, Western developed countries are not only observing where China is headed but also reflecting on what they may have missed. Developing nations are examining what kinds of urban lifestyles and industrial development can become a reality, and whether the path to industrialization must necessarily follow the old path of "polluting first, then cleaning up." Shenzhen is not the sole answer to the future, yet it proves there is more than one path forward. Over the past week, Shenzhen has undoubtedly stood at the center of the world's spotlight. In media reports from around the globe - ranging from its densely packed skyscrapers to self-driving taxis on the streets - Shenzhen has been portrayed as a "futuristic city." Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney praised Shenzhen, saying, "The future is designed here, tested here and built here." US President Donald Trump noted that Shenzhen is "clean" and "immaculate," adding that, in contrast, the development and governance of some US cities are "embarrassing." Peruvian President Keiko Fujimori stated that "there is no doubt that we can learn from Shenzhen" in its approach to smart and digital urban governance. On overseas social media platforms, "Shenzhen" continues to dominate the feed. One netizen wrote, "This might be the most futuristic city I've ever visited in my life," while another added, "I wish my country could have a Shenzhen too." Why has a once remote fishing village attracted so much attention? When the world talks about Shenzhen, what exactly are they talking about? Perhaps the answer lies in one word: future. Seen from within China, Shenzhen embodies the concrete form of Chinese modernization, offering a vivid interpretation of the idea that "the next 'China' is still China." When the Special Economic Zone was established in 1980, Shenzhen's population was less than 30,000. Now, it has developed into a modern international metropolis and "super hub" with a population of over 18 million. Today, people here see self-driving cars cruising the streets, drone deliveries becoming part of daily life, robots operating in factories and shopping malls, and companies like Huawei, BYD, DJI, and Tencent making their mark on the global market. Behind these achievements lie China's sustained investment and stable planning - rooted in its own development and oriented toward the future - and, ultimately, a people-centered approach to development. Viewed from the world's perspective, Western developed countries are not only observing where China is headed but also reflecting on what they may have missed. A key reason why Trump's assessment of Shenzhen's roads and urban environment sparked debate in US public opinion is that it touched on the long-standing challenges of urban governance facing American society. Road maintenance, public transportation, and environmental sanitation - these seemingly ordinary public services are, in fact, persistent challenges that many countries struggle to address. Developing nations, meanwhile, are examining what kinds of urban lifestyles and industrial development can become a reality, and whether the path to industrialization must necessarily follow the old path of "polluting first, then cleaning up." Whether developed or developing, countries are beginning to consider whether they should pursue this kind of future. Shenzhen is not the sole answer to the future, yet it proves that there is more than one path forward. Different countries have different historical traditions, cultural practices, resource endowments, and social systems; there can be no single "standard answer" for urban modernization. Nor is Shenzhen's path a template that can be simply replicated. Its significance lies in demonstrating that openness can spur innovation, industry can foster technology, technology can improve lives, and global cooperation can expand the scope for development. Chilean President Jose Antonio Kast remarked, "Shenzhen's transformation reminds us that progress is not a miracle but a resolution." Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, drawing on his experiences from visits in 1998 and 2026, remarked that if someone were to place photographs from then and now side by side, it was almost impossible to believe they were of the same place. This demonstrates that the future can be continuously shaped through reform, opening-up, and relentless exploration. What the world needs is not a replica of Shenzhen, but more cities like Shenzhen that can shape their own futures. Today, Shenzhen has evolved from a place where the Chinese people learned about the world through the "window of the world" to a place where the world observes China and envisions the future. In just over 40 years, Shenzhen has traversed a journey that took some major international metropolises abroad more than a century to complete, proving that modernization does not follow a single predetermined path. A late-developing economy can fully forge its own path - one that balances efficiency with people's livelihoods, and vitality with order. This demonstrates that the "future" is not merely a fixed blueprint. Every country and every civilization can draw upon its own historical traditions, social structures, and resource endowments to find a "future blueprint" that suits it best. British urban planning scholar Peter Hall once wrote Cities of Tomorrow, which traces urban planning practices from the late 19th century to the late 20th century - a work in which London, New York, Paris, and Chicago frequently feature. Today, one "city of tomorrow" after another is emerging across China. We welcome more countries, enterprises, research institutions, and innovators to come to Shenzhen. Rather than merely viewing a single "pre-existing model," we can strive to build more models and explore abundant future forms of AI, green development, urban governance, public services, and industrial cooperation. Shenzhen's story is far from finished, and the exploration of Chinese modernization is still underway. The invitation Shenzhen extends to the world is this: China is willing to showcase its own future, and welcomes the world to bring its own dreams here to jointly create even more bright futures.

item.title: Shenzhou-23 crew prepares for 'space rendezvous' as Shenzhou-24 mission nears launch
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-22 21:23:00
The Shenzhou-23 crew aboard China's space station prepares to welcome the incoming Shenzhou-24 crew. Screenshot from CCTV News The Shenzhou-23 crew aboard China's Space Station is making preparations to welcome the incoming Shenzhou-24 crew while continuing to carry out a range of scientific experiments, CCTV News reported on Sunday. The combination of the Shenzhou-24 spacecraft and its Long March-2F carrier rocket was transferred to the launch area on November 17 and is scheduled for launch at an appropriate time in the coming days, according to a release from the China Manned Space Agency (CMSA). With the mission approaching, the space station is preparing for a special "space rendezvous" as the two crews prepare to meet in orbit. Despite the upcoming crew rotation, the three Shenzhou-23 astronauts remain engaged in their scheduled scientific research. In the field of microgravity physics, they have completed the retrieval of samples from the variable gravity science experiment cabinet, replaced and disposed of samples in the high-temperature materials science experiment cabinet, and replaced components of an inertial particle experiment device in the on-orbit maintenance and assembly operation cabinet. In the field of space technology and applications, the crew has also installed samples for two research projects focusing on microbial prevention and control materials, as well as rapid microbial detection and technical protection. Preparing for the arrival of a new crew involves more than completing scientific tasks. The Shenzhou-23 crew has been cleaning the station's interior and putting its living quarters in order to ensure that the orbital outpost is ready to accommodate the newcomers, per CCTV News. Once the Shenzhou-24 crew arrives, the number of astronauts aboard the space station will increase from three to six for a period of time, significantly raising demand for essential resources such as oxygen and water. To accommodate the additional crew members, the astronauts must adjust settings for the station's operating systems and living facilities in advance. These preparations include configuring lighting in sleeping areas, setting up the urine and feces collection equipment in the space station's toilets, checking the power supply to galley equipment, and adjusting the cabin's environmental control systems to ensure that the facilities can support six astronauts simultaneously. The station's regenerative life support system will play a crucial role in meeting the increased demand. Technologies such as oxygen generation through water electrolysis, carbon dioxide removal and urine processing enable the station to recycle resources and reduce its dependence on supplies delivered from Earth, supporting long-term human presence in orbit. The upcoming crew rotation will also mark a milestone in international space cooperation. A Pakistani astronaut will join the Shenzhou-24 mission as a payload specialist and travel to China's space station, marking the first time that Chinese and foreign astronauts will participate in a joint spaceflight mission under China's manned space program. The visit will also make him the first foreign astronaut to enter the China space station, according to CCTV News. The 'space rendezvous' of the two crews will be followed by a special meal together in orbit. At the same time, the Shenzhou-23 crew is making preparations for its eventual return to Earth. These include collecting cabin gas, microbial and water samples, retrieving experimental samples and payloads to be brought back to Earth, and clearing away waste and personal belongings. According to the mission arrangements, one member of the Shenzhou-23 crew will remain aboard the space station after the crew transition, although the astronaut's identity has not yet been announced, CCTV News reported. The Shenzhou-24 crewed mission has also entered its final preparatory stage. On Saturday, the mission completed its final full-system rehearsal, while the launch site completed preparations for the upcoming launch, as reported by the Xinhua News Agency. Global Times

item.title: What are Western media concealing by shifting the climate spotlight to China?
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-22 21:23:00
COP31 president and senior officials arrive for a session during the United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP31) at the Antalya Expo Center in Antalya, Turkey, on November 22, 2026. Photo: VCG As the extended negotiations of COP31 in Antalya, Turkey, drag on, questions - such as why Beijing is "unwilling to take on a leadership role" on climate issues - are frequently raised in Western media. These biased questions carry the implicit assumption that leadership means bearing more obligations than others, and that China's low-key posture is a major factor hindering progress. Both assumptions deserve scrutiny. The real bottleneck in global climate governance is no longer a lack of specific targets, but the failure to implement them. The latest draft text removed explicit language on phasing out coal, oil and gas. Negotiations on finance, adaptation and a just transition remain deadlocked. Ambition on paper has outpaced real economic action. Against this backdrop, Western media have turned their attention to China, posing a question whose answer they already know: Why is Beijing "unwilling to take on a leadership role" on climate issues? By questioning why China is "so low-key," they divert attention from the responsibilities the West itself should shoulder on climate issues. Deutsche Welle (DW), citing a Reuters analysis, noted that after Washington retreated in climate diplomacy, many had hoped China would "fill this gap." However, Beijing has ruled out hosting COP33 in 2028 and adopted a "consistently low-key" posture in Antalya. At the same time, the debate over whether China should still be regarded as a developing country has heated up again. China's specific 2035 climate goals, announced in September 2025, include a 7 to 10 percent net emissions reduction from peak levels, over 30 percent non-fossil energy, 3,600 gigawatts of installed capacity for wind and solar power, over 24 billion cubic meters of forest stock volume, and the basic establishment of a climate-adaptive society. The same standards should apply to everyone. Developed countries pledged to mobilize $100 billion per year in climate finance for developing countries. According to OECD data, these countries reached about $116 billion in 2022, the first year the target was met; however, questions remain about how loans are counted and whether such support is predictable. Adaptation finance - the type most needed by vulnerable countries - has consistently accounted for a smaller share than mitigation finance (the latest data show that its absolute amount is even declining). When the countries least responsible for emissions struggle to obtain the funds already promised, it raises a question: Why do Western media turn the spotlight on China rather than discuss their own unfulfilled commitments? In addition, Western governments call on China to "do more" on climate change while imposing tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles (EVs), batteries and solar products. The EU's countervailing duties on Chinese EVs and US tariffs on EVs, batteries, and solar modules are justified on grounds such as subsidies, overcapacity, and supply chain security. If rapidly deploying the lowest-cost clean technologies is key to cutting global emissions, then trade barriers that obstruct such deployment actually harm the climate goals Western governments claim to pursue. That is why China's push for liberalizing trade in green products in Antalya should be viewed in context. This demand aims to open markets for low-cost clean technologies. Whether this effort succeeds will depend on whether importing countries are willing to recognize that cheaper clean technologies are a climate asset, and whether they will justify any restrictive measures with evidence rather than defend them on the assumption that "Chinese products are inherently suspect." The installed capacity figures repeatedly cited by Western media are, in fact, a question of how to understand the speed and quality of China's development. China is making enormous efforts to meet its targets. Installed capacity is "capacity building" and a "necessary precondition" for the energy transition. The key lies not in the installed capacity numbers themselves, but in the quality of subsequent implementation and the supporting systems. This is essential for correctly understanding China's position on climate issues. What global emissions reduction truly needs is not a new label but the honoring of existing commitments: Developed countries providing financial support, substantially cutting emissions, and opening green technology markets. China will fulfill its due responsibilities and achieve its emissions reduction targets. Developing countries need to improve the quality and speed of green economy development. Each should shoulder its own responsibility and move forward together.

item.title: Portable 'Wi-Fi' terminals help China's military units maintain battlefield connectivity on the move
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-22 21:11:00
Photo: PLA Daily A lightweight communication terminal, weighing less than 3 kilograms, is helping Chinese military units maintain communication links - like a portable Wi-Fi - as they maneuver between battlefield positions, offering a more flexible alternative to the time-consuming deployment of traditional communication cables, read a PLA Daily report on Sunday. The portable network and communications terminal, developed by a unit of the People's Liberation Army (PLA) Information Support Force, can be rapidly deployed to establish wireless connections between command terminals and frontline units, allowing information to be transmitted without waiting for communication cables to be laid again after a position change. In a recent joint training exercise, a PLA Air Force firepower unit received an order to relocate shortly after having completed a round of live-fire exercises. While a communications support team was preparing to carry conventional fiber-optic cables to the new position, an advance team reported that the portable terminal had already been set up, with the command communications link established. By the time the cable-laying team arrived, the firepower unit had completed a simulated strike and was preparing to move again, the PLA Daily reported. The development addresses a long-standing challenge in battlefield communications support. Under traditional arrangements, communications personnel had to retrieve and re-deploy cables whenever combat units changed positions, a process that required considerable manpower and time and could leave units temporarily without communications. Military commentator Song Zhongping told the Global Times on Sunday that mobile networking can significantly improve the speed and flexibility of communications support compared with conventional cable-based deployment. "Mobile networking, as the name suggests, means no longer having to lay extensive networks of cables as was traditionally done. The traditional approach consumes considerable manpower, material resources and financial resources, while its efficiency and ability to respond rapidly are limited," Song told the Global Times. By deploying mobile communications equipment, including base stations, military units can establish communications and command networks more quickly and move these capabilities to areas where they are needed, Song noted. "For a military force to respond rapidly, what needs to come first is not just logistics, but also command and communications," Song said. "Without that, it is impossible to achieve connectivity and interoperability across the entire force." According to the PLA Daily report, the portable terminals can be deployed at multiple locations to form a mobile networking cluster, rather than relying on a single communications node or fixed position. During another training exercise involving the seizure of key positions, an advance unit maneuvered through difficult terrain and areas with dense electromagnetic interference. Using multiple portable terminals, the unit established a mobile network while moving and filled gaps in communications coverage. When a reconnaissance team identified a simulated enemy firepower position, target information was transmitted through the mobile network to several dispersed firepower units. The units then coordinated their simulated strikes based on a shared, real-time operational picture. The communications links remained operational throughout the exercise, the PLA Daily report said. Song said the use of multiple interconnected nodes can improve the resilience of battlefield communications by providing redundancy. "Communications on the battlefield cannot rely entirely on a single node. Multiple nodes are needed, with several portable mobile communications terminals deployed redundantly to ensure that the entire communications network remains secure and reliable," Song told the Global Times. However, the shift toward wireless networking also brings security challenges that cannot be overlooked. Song noted that wireless communications inevitably involve the transmission of radio signals, creating the possibility that communications could be intercepted or information disclosed. Encryption and other security safeguards are therefore essential to mobile military communications systems. "How to prevent information from being leaked is the core challenge facing mobile and network-based communications," he said. The PLA Daily report also stressed that the portable terminals are not intended to replace wired communications. Instead, the unit is exploring a complementary model combining fixed and mobile systems: Wired networks are used at established positions, where reliability and resistance to interference are priorities, while portable equipment is deployed for temporary maneuvers and field operations, where rapid setup and filling coverage gaps are more important. The unit has also incorporated challenging conditions, including strong electromagnetic interference and difficult terrain, into routine training to test equipment performance and refine its networking methods. Looking ahead, Song said military communications systems would continue to evolve alongside advances in technology, with more sophisticated encryption methods and new forms of portable, distributed communications equipment potentially improving their security and reliability. "New technologies will continue to replace older ones, but the ultimate goal remains ensuring that communications are reliable and secure, with security always coming first," he said.

item.title: China urges US to revoke proposed telecom restrictions, warns of damage to bilateral ties
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-22 20:59:00
Logos of China's three major telecom operators China Telecom, China Unicom, and China Mobile Schematic photo: VCG China's Ministry of Commerce (MOFCOM) on Sunday called on the US to revoke proposed restrictions on Chinese telecom operators' direct access to US phone numbers, saying the move violates the principles of non-discrimination and fair competition. The response came after the US Federal Communications Commission (FCC) voted on Thursday to bar China Mobile, China Telecom, and China Unicom from directly obtaining US phone numbers for internet-based calls. The FCC had previously barred the three operators from providing international telecommunications services in the US, Reuters reported. Chinese experts warned that the US move reflects Washington's growing tendency to overstretch the concept of national security and politicize normal economic and trade activities. While its direct financial impact on major Chinese telecom operators would be limited, the restrictions could raise costs for cross-border businesses, undermine market competition and technological cooperation, and erode mutual trust at a time when the two countries are seeking to stabilize bilateral economic and trade relations. Unjustified restrictions In a statement released on Sunday, MOFCOM said the US FCC abused its regulatory powers and overstretched the concept of national security while making groundless accusations against Chinese telecom companies and maliciously undermining their operations in the US, a commerce ministry spokesperson noted in response to a media query. The FCC has recently continued to push to decouple and sever supply chains between China and the US in telecommunications, communications, testing, and certification, the spokesperson added. This runs counter to the important consensus reached by the two heads of state and undermines the stability of China-US economic and trade relations, the spokesperson said. China urges the US to immediately rescind the measures and return to the right way of resolving issues through consultations, the spokesperson said, noting that China will take necessary measures to firmly safeguard its own interests. The FCC claimed that the restrictions were intended to address "national security" concerns and prevent scam-related robocalls. Zhou Mi, a senior research fellow at the Chinese Academy of International Trade and Economic Cooperation, told the Global Times on Sunday that the US restrictions would interfere with normal market competition, erect discriminatory barriers against Chinese telecom operators, and undermine fair competition in the telecommunications industry. If implemented, the measures would prevent affected Chinese operators from directly providing certain internet-based telephone services to US customers, restricting their ability to expand in the American market. But the consequences would extend beyond Chinese companies, Zhou said. By restricting competition, the US risks hurting its own consumers, limiting their choices and putting greater pressure on service prices and quality, Zhou said. "Excluding market participants could weaken incentives for investment and innovation, ultimately hindering technological progress," he added. Ma Jihua, a veteran telecom industry analyst, told the Global Times that the restrictions would have a negligible direct impact on the revenues of China's three major telecom operators, given their already limited business presence in the US. The measure does not amount to a blanket ban on calls between the two countries but targets Chinese operators' direct access to US numbering resources, he explained. However, Ma warned that the limited financial impact on Chinese operators did not mean the restrictions would come without costs for the US. Businesses relying on cross-border internet-based voice services, including exporters, e-commerce companies, and overseas offices, could face higher costs and longer service activation times if forced to obtain numbering services through US-based providers. While ordinary US consumers were unlikely to face immediate disruption to international calls, higher operating and compliance costs could eventually be passed on to US businesses and then consumers, Ma said. Ma also questioned the effectiveness of the restrictions in combating telecom fraud, noting that scammers do not rely solely on direct access to US telephone numbering resources. They could still make fraudulent calls through third-party providers, internet-based calling services, or caller ID spoofing. Simply restricting Chinese telecom operators' direct access to US numbers may therefore do little to curb such activities. He further warned that the restrictions could force legitimate telecommunications services to rely on more third-party providers, making communication channels more complex. With more intermediaries involved, regulators could face greater difficulties tracing the origins of suspicious calls and identifying those responsible. Consensus needs action The latest US restrictions contrast with recent efforts by Beijing and Washington to stabilize bilateral relations and expand economic cooperation. During the November 19 meeting in Shenzhen on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Economic Leaders' Meeting, the two countries' heads of state agreed to develop an action plan for a constructive relationship of strategic stability, according to the Chinese Foreign Ministry. At the meeting, China called for a longer list of cooperation and a shorter list of problems and stressed that differences that cannot be resolved for the time being should be managed in a constructive way, and escalation should be prevented. The talks followed the first meeting of the bilateral trade council on November 13, when officials discussed tariffs and agricultural trade and agreed to maintain communication. Earlier on October 29, the FCC had voted to bar Chinese laboratories from testing electronics for the US market. According to Ma, the latest measures reflected an expansion of US restrictions beyond hardware and equipment to telecommunications numbering resources and computing power. Such an approach could disrupt the global division of labor in telecommunications and raise costs for multinational businesses, Ma said. He warned that continued restrictions could encourage companies to develop alternative communications and computing systems, potentially weakening the global influence of US technology standards. The restrictions could undermine the mutual trust needed to implement the leaders' consensus and complicate efforts to resolve existing disputes and address emerging technological challenges, Zhou said. Some US politicians should demonstrate their commitment to cooperation through concrete actions rather than allowing unilateral restrictions to erode mutual trust, Chinese analysts stressed.

item.title: Chinese, Vietnamese navies complete 41st joint patrol in Beibu Gulf; move boosts maritime trust and risk control: expert
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-22 20:47:00
Photo: PLA Navy The Chinese and Vietnamese navies have successfully completed their 41st joint patrol in the Beibu Gulf over two days, covering 351 nautical miles in 32 hours and including a joint maritime search-and-rescue drill, the PLA Daily reported on Sunday. China and Vietnam's joint naval patrols as well as joint coast guard operations could help manage risks, foster mutual trust and resolve maritime differences. By boosting cooperation in the Beibu Gulf and upholding maritime security and order, the two sides are also consolidating cooperation in fisheries, shipping and maritime search and rescue, and contributing to peace, stability and development across the region, according to a Chinese military expert. During the joint patrol, China deployed the naval vessels Wuzhou and Enshi, while Vietnam sent two naval vessels to participate. The Chinese and Vietnamese vessels arrived in their designated patrol area in the Beibu Gulf on Friday. After establishing communications, the two sides patrolled in two parallel columns along the China-Vietnam demarcation line in the gulf, according to the PLA Daily. During the operation, the two sides transferred command authority in stages and exchanged data on courses, speeds and other operational details, maintaining real-time awareness of the maritime situation. On Saturday, the joint patrol fleet held a search-and-rescue drill simulating two fishing vessels in distress in the Beibu Gulf. After being informed that crew members had fallen overboard, the fleet adjusted its course and speed, drew up search-and-rescue plan and used multiple search methods to accurately locate and rescue the personnel in the water. After the exercise, the fleet practiced coordinated formation changes under agreed rules for alternating command, including single-column, single-line-abreast and double-column formations. Both sides maintained close communication and demonstrated smooth coordination throughout the drills. After completing all scheduled drills, the Chinese and Vietnamese vessels separated and departed in different directions. Personnel from both sides lined up in their respective areas and waved goodbye, marking the successful conclusion of the 41st China-Vietnam joint patrol. The choice of vessels on Chinese side underscores the non-confrontational nature of the joint patrols, which focus on maritime risk management, emergency response and confidence-building rather than military deterrence, Song Zhongping, a military affairs expert, told the Global Times on Sunday. The rotating command arrangement also reflects both sides' equal sovereign status while enhancing interoperability, mutual understanding and coordination, said Song. The PLA Daily cited a Chinese commander as saying that adding exercises to the joint patrol enhanced the two navies' ability to conduct coordinated operations and promoted professional exchanges and practical cooperation between the two sides. The China-Vietnam joint patrols in the Beibu Gulf are friendly exchanges conducted by the two militaries under relevant agreements and annual plans. The report said the patrols help strengthen friendship between the two countries, deepen mutual trust between the two militaries, and effectively enhancing both sides' ability to respond jointly to maritime emergencies and safeguard maritime security and stability. Song noted that China and Vietnam conduct joint naval patrols and coast guard law enforcement operations through separate, parallel mechanisms in the Beibu Gulf to manage maritime differences and prevent disputes from escalating. Regular communication channels, coordinated response protocols and frontline cooperation help reduce miscalculations, build military trust and strengthen crisis management. Since the signing of the Agreement on Joint Patrols by the Navies of China and Vietnam in the Beibu Gulf in 2005, these patrols have served as a stable platform for communication, helping both sides deepen cooperation and enhance strategic mutual trust, according to the Xinhua News Agency. The Chinese and Vietnamese coast guards conducted their first joint patrol in the Beibu Gulf for 2026 from April 22 to 24, marking the 30th joint patrol by the two countries' maritime law enforcement agencies since 2006. By strengthening cooperation in the Beibu Gulf, China and Vietnam are also upholding the spirit of the Declaration on the Conduct of Parties in the South China Sea (DOC), safeguarding maritime security and stability, and advancing cooperation in fisheries, shipping and search and rescue, said Song. Such coordination also supports broader economic and trade ties between the two countries, helping contain risks, build mutual trust and promote peace and development in the South China Sea and across Southeast Asia, the expert said.

item.title: Mainland drama online fan event draws 260,000 views; DPP authorities criticized for blocking cross-Straits cultural exchange
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-22 20:31:00
Zhang's still in Pursuit of Jade Photo: Courtesy of Douban An online fan meeting for Pursuit of Jade , a Chinese mainland costume drama popular in Taiwan this year, drew 260,000 views over the weekend. The event sparked criticism of the island authorities' political interference in cross-Straits cultural exchanges, after the lead actor Zhang Linghe was previously denied permission to hold an in-person event there. Chinese mainland dramas, films and short videos, particularly those showcasing traditional Chinese culture, have resonated strongly with audiences in Taiwan, reflecting years of cross-Straits cultural exchanges, said a senior cross-Straits expert. However, amid worsening cross-Straits ties, the Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) authorities' hostile policy toward the mainland and pursuit of Taiwan independence have led to tighter restrictions on cultural and other people-to-people exchanges, making the limited interactions that remain a focus of public attention. The lead actors of Pursuit of Jade, Zhang Linghe and Tian Xiwei, held an online fan meeting on Saturday. The two actors shared behind-the-scenes stories and discussed their hometowns with fans across the Straits, with related topics also trending on Sina Weibo, Taiwan-based media udn.com reported. Fans in Taiwan prepared a selection of local specialties as gifts for Zhang and Tian, including peanut brittle, pineapple cakes and Mazu-themed mystery boxes, and invited them to visit the island. The two actors said they hoped to meet their fans in person in the island, chatting about Tainan's famous beef soup and local night markets during the livestream, udn.com reported. However, Zhang was previously denied permission to hold an in-person fan meeting in Taiwan, with the Taiwan's so-called Mainland Affairs Council citing his alleged "demeaning" remarks about the island's status and insufficient details about the event's nature and purpose, the Xinhua News Agency reported. Notably, Chinese mainland TV series have built a substantial audience in Taiwan, while fans in Taiwan have also shown enthusiasm to meet mainland actors in person. Since 2022, TV stations in Taiwan have broadcast The Legend of Zhen Huan around the clock throughout the Chinese New Year holidays. The annual broadcasts have since sparked a renewed viewing craze each year. Statistics show that in 2025, the drama was aired continuously, 24 hours a day, for 26 consecutive days, attracting a record 20.31 million views. An editorial in Taiwan region's media outlet Want Daily said the popularity of Chinese mainland dramas in Taiwan and the consistently high ratings received by Taiwanese dramas on the mainland's Douban review platform reflects shared viewing preferences and deep-rooted cultural ties across the Taiwan Straits. It said film and television works remain an important bridge for overcoming differences and bringing people on both sides closer. The drama's popularity in the island of Taiwan could strengthen local audiences' affinity for Chinese culture and their Chinese identity, which the DPP authorities view as running counter to their pro-independence agenda, prompting restrictions on cross-Straits exchanges, Wang Jianmin, a senior cross-Straits expert at Minnan Normal University in Fujian Province, told the Global Times on Sunday. The DPP authorities have increasingly portrayed cultural, film and artistic exchanges as "united front work," making meaningful cross-Straits interactions difficult. The Taiwan Affairs Office of the State Council on October 21 condemned DPP authorities for rejecting Zhang's application to visit the island for cultural exchange activities, including a fan meeting. Speaking at a regular press briefing on October 21, Zhang Han, a spokesperson for the mainland office, said visits by Chinese mainland performers for cultural exchanges were welcomed and anticipated by people on both sides of the Taiwan Straits, and would help foster mutual understanding. Zhang noted that the DPP authorities had rejected the application for political reasons, disregarding the wishes of people in Taiwan, particularly young people. Such restrictions undermine cross-Straits cultural exchanges and run counter to the aspirations of people in Taiwan, she added. The spokesperson urged the DPP authorities to abandon political manipulation and remove unreasonable restrictions to facilitate cultural exchanges.

item.title: COP31 fails to reach consensus on Antalya Pact as key deal rejected
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-22 20:10:00
COP31 President Murat Kurum (center) leaves a closing plenary session at the COP31 UN Climate Summit in Antalya, Turkey, on November 22, 2026. The 31st COP31 failed to reach a consensus on the Antalya Pact. Photo: VCG The COP31 climate talks headed for a historic defeat on Sunday after the EU and other countries refused to endorse a pact that omitted fossil fuels as the summit lurched into record overtime in Turkey. "We will not endorse a cover decision, or an Antalya Pact, that does not even mention fossil fuels, which is the key driver of climate change," said Ireland's climate minister, Darragh O'Brien, whose country holds the rotating EU presidency, Le Monde reported on Sunday. Chinese experts warned that growing green trade protectionism and attempts to shift climate responsibilities risk undermining global climate action, while highlighting China's contributions to making clean energy technologies more affordable worldwide. The organizers released a final deal early on Sunday morning, Antalya local time, which keeps a call to electrify the global economy but makes no mention of fossil fuels despite a fierce backlash when they were stripped from an earlier proposal, according to the Australian broadcaster ABC. The developments came as a new study compiled by the Chinese Research Academy of Environmental Sciences (CRAES) and the Institute of Public & Environmental Affairs (IPE), obtained by the Global Times, estimated that China's photovoltaic industry had helped reduce global solar module procurement costs by approximately $175.3 billion between 2011 and 2025, underscoring the practical importance of affordable clean energy technologies to the global green transition. Overtime negotiations expose divisions The latest compromise proposal came after negotiations stretched beyond their scheduled Friday conclusion and continued into the early hours of Sunday. Despite mounting pressure from countries demanding stronger commitments on fossil fuels, the revised document again omitted explicit references to coal, oil, and gas, instead referring to an agreement reached at COP28 in Dubai in 2023 on transitioning away from fossil fuels, AFP reported Sunday. The proposal also retained language supporting the expansion of clean energy and the acceleration of carbon capture and storage technologies, although the latter remained controversial among countries concerned about their costs and effectiveness. The draft had not secured consensus among nearly 200 participating delegations and the COP31 failed to reach consensus on the Antalya Pact on Sunday. While the latest COP31 draft retained the goal of tripling adaptation finance by 2035, it omitted an earlier proposal to provide at least $120 billion annually to developing countries, leaving key questions over funding levels and implementation unresolved, according to media reports. "The deadlock at COP31 may appear to center on disagreements over the transition away from fossil fuels and the allocation of climate finance, but at a deeper level, it reflects a serious imbalance between responsibilities and interests in global climate governance. Developed countries are urging developing nations to accelerate emissions reductions while failing to take sufficient action on financial support and technology transfer," Chen Hong, director of the Institute of Country and Region Studies at the School of Foreign Languages, East China Normal University, told the Global Times on Sunday. Ambitions versus barriers The 35 percent electrification target retained in the latest COP31 draft echoed a goal supported by China and Australia in their November 20 joint statement on climate change and the clean energy transition. The statement emphasized that measures taken to combat climate change should not constitute arbitrary or unjustifiable discrimination or disguised restrictions on international trade, reaffirming a principle enshrined in the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change. In a Saturday report, The Guardian highlighted China's willingness to share its experience in expanding clean energy technologies and reducing their costs, while noting Chinese concerns over US tariffs and the European Union's Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism, or CBAM. A study published by the United Nations Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD) in 2021 found that the introduction of a CBAM results in declines in exports in developing countries in favor of developed countries, which tend to have less carbon-intensive production processes. "Some Western countries are applying obvious double standards in their green policies. On one hand, they call for urgent climate action and an accelerated energy transition. On the other hand, they erect trade barriers against Chinese electric vehicles, solar products, and other green technologies," Chen said. "The irony is that, in trying to protect their own green industries, these countries are actually driving up the cost of the global green transition. The consequences extend beyond Chinese companies, affecting developing countries' access to affordable clean energy technologies," he added. A study jointly released during COP31 by CRAES and IPE estimated that China's photovoltaic industry helped avoid approximately 4.91 billion tons of carbon dioxide equivalent emissions between 2015 and 2025 through domestic installations and overseas module exports. Ma Jun, director of the IPE, who attended the COP31 summit in Turkey as an observer, told the Global Times on Sunday that the report quantified the significant contribution of China's photovoltaic industry to global climate action, offering a concrete example of how Chinese green technologies are delivering global public goods. He added that China's affordable and accessible green technologies are helping countries, particularly those in the Global South, address the challenge of overshooting global climate targets, while providing practical, financially viable, and scalable solutions for climate mitigation and adaptation. Such contributions are enabling developing countries to pursue their climate goals in a more affordable and sustainable manner, he said. Without China's contributions, the global cost of tackling climate change and advancing climate governance would be significantly higher, Ma noted. COP31 president and senior officials arrive for a session during the United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP31) at the Antalya Expo Center in Antalya, Turkey, on November 22, 2026. Photo: VCG Great contribution Meanwhile, the growing international recognition of China's role in clean energy development has prompted another debate over how climate responsibilities should be distributed. In a Friday analysis titled "Why China is unwilling to be the world's next climate leader," Reuters said China should assume a greater international climate leadership role, citing its position as the world's largest annual greenhouse gas emitter and a major supplier of clean energy technologies such as solar panels, wind turbines, and electric vehicles. The report also cited China's continued alignment with developing countries on climate finance and referred to expectations from some climate-vulnerable nations for Beijing to play a more prominent role. The contrast between recognition of China's technological contributions and calls for it to shoulder greater climate responsibilities illustrates a broader challenge facing international climate governance. However, the question of climate responsibility involves more than current annual emissions or industrial capacity. Under the Paris Agreement, countries' climate actions are guided by the principle of equity and common but differentiated responsibilities and respective capabilities, in light of different national circumstances. China's contributions to global climate action should be viewed in their proper context, Ma said. Through ambitious domestic climate initiatives, large-scale development and deployment of clean energy technologies, efforts to drive down renewable energy costs, and South-South cooperation, China has made substantial contributions to the global climate response. However, these voluntary contributions should not be conflated with the historical responsibilities and climate finance obligations of developed countries under the international climate framework, he stressed. Ma further noted that assessments of climate responsibility should take into account historical cumulative emissions, per capita emissions, different stages of development, and countries' respective capabilities, rather than overlooking the principle of equity and differentiated responsibilities. Chinese experts emphasized that advancing global climate action requires not only ambitious targets but also affordable technologies, adequate financial support, and a fair distribution of responsibilities.

item.title: New dinosaur fossil discovery fills gap in Early Cretaceous fossil record in Inner Mongolia, North China
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-22 17:16:00
Fossil localities and specimen photographs Photo: Inner Mongolia Museum of Natural History Digital reconstruction of the dentary Photo: Inner Mongolia Museum of Natural History Chinese researchers have discovered the first Early Cretaceous hadrosauroid dinosaur fossil in the Erlian Basin in North China's Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region. The study, published in the international paleontological journal Fossil Record, fills a gap in the region's fossil record and offers new clues to the early evolution and diversification of the herbivorous dinosaur group. The study, titled "The First Hadrosauroid Dinosaur from the Lower Cretaceous of the Erlian Basin, Inner Mongolia, China," was led by the Inner Mongolia Museum of Natural History, with participation from the Institute of Vertebrate Paleontology and Paleoanthropology of the Chinese Academy of Sciences and Shenyang Normal University, among other institutions. Unearthed in Ejin Horo township, East Ujimqin banner, the fossil is the first recorded hadrosauroid specimen from the Lower Cretaceous strata of the Erlian Basin. The specimen is now housed at the Inner Mongolia Museum of Natural History, comprising a left dentary, teeth, vertebrae, toe bones and several bone fragments. Although fragmented and scattered, the bones were found concentrated in a relatively small area, suggesting that the specimen was buried close to its original position, according to preliminary assessments. Hadrosauroids were among the most abundant groups of herbivorous dinosaurs of the Cretaceous Period. Their earliest known fossils date back to the Early Cretaceous, and the group reached its peak diversity in the Late Cretaceous before spreading worldwide. Early Cretaceous hadrosauroid fossils have mainly been found in East Asia, including western Liaoning Province, Mazongshan in Gansu Province, the Alxa-Bayannur region of western Inner Mongolia and the eastern Gobi Desert in Mongolia. Most studies suggest that Asia was the center of origin and early diversification and dispersal of hadrosauroids. Located between these fossil-rich regions, the Erlian Basin had previously yielded no reported Early Cretaceous hadrosauroid fossils. The discovery has filled a gap in the fossil record between these localities, indicating that hadrosauroids were already inhabiting the basin during the Early Cretaceous. Researchers found that the new specimen exhibits a combination of primitive and more advanced traits. It retains primitive features of early ornithopod dinosaurs, such as accessory ridges on both the mesial and distal sides of the primary ridge on its upper jaw teeth. It also displays several features closer to those of hadrosaurids, including an elongated toothless region at the front of the dentary, more tooth positions and a primary ridge positioned near the center of the teeth. These traits provide important clues for reconstructing the early evolutionary sequence of key features in hadrosaurids and suggest that hadrosauroids had already developed considerable diversity during the Early Cretaceous. Despite the incomplete preservation of the specimen, its distinctive combination of morphological features suggests that it may represent a new genus and species of hadrosauroid outside the hadrosaurid family. More systematic field surveys and rescue excavations aimed at obtaining more complete fossil material will be essential for determining the specimen's exact taxonomic position and clarifying how key hadrosauroid traits evolved. The fossil was recovered through a rescue excavation conducted under a project commissioned by the department of natural resources of the Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region. In recent years, the Inner Mongolia Museum of Natural History has stepped up efforts to survey regional fossil resources, carry out rescue excavations, restore specimens, develop joint research platforms and promote public science education.
